title: I know that my redeemer lives (Job 19:25–27)
hook: in the depths, Job reaches for hope anyway

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eliphaz and the comfort that hurt. Your line: don't explain their pain.

By chapter nineteen, it's bad. The friends have stopped being gentle. Job says his brothers keep their distance, his servants ignore him, his breath is strange to his own wife, and little children mock him when he stands up. "Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends; for the hand of God hath touched me." Nobody does. Then he wishes for something odd: that his words could be carved with an iron pen into rock, filled in with lead, so someone someday would know what he said. His wish came true. What he says next is still read aloud and sung.
screen: `FRIENDS GONE, FAMILY DISTANT.` → `CARVE MY WORDS IN ROCK.` → `THE WISH CAME TRUE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth." The Hebrew word for redeemer is go'el, and it's a family word before it's a church word. A go'el was your nearest relative with a duty to you. If debt forced you to sell your land, your go'el bought it back. If you were sold into slavery, your go'el paid to free you. If you were killed, your go'el made sure your blood didn't go unanswered. In the book of Ruth, Boaz is the go'el who buys back a family's land and marries the widow Ruth. So when Job, abandoned by family and friends, says my go'el lives, he's saying: somebody is still on my side, and will stand up for me at the end, even if nobody here will. Who is it? Readers have heard it differently. Christian tradition hears Christ: the redeemer who lives and stands on the earth at the last day. Handel set it to music in Messiah, and the Book of Common Prayer sets it among the sentences that open its burial service. Jewish commentators have heard God himself as Job's defender. Some scholars think Job meant a heavenly witness, the advocate he mentions a few chapters earlier. And the next verse is hard to translate: in my flesh shall I see God, or without my flesh. The King James chose "yet in my flesh shall I see God." Either way, a man at the bottom reaches up anyway.
screen: `GO'EL: THE FAMILY REDEEMER` · `BUYS BACK LAND, FREES THE SLAVE` · `CHRIST, GOD, OR A HEAVENLY WITNESS` · `A HOPE CARVED IN ROCK` · then, large: `I KNOW THAT MY REDEEMER LIVETH.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you hope for that you can't make happen yourself: healing, a reconciliation, someone coming home, justice. Hold it the way Job holds his, not because the evidence is good, but because you refuse to let go. If you pray, say his line slowly, I know that my redeemer liveth; if not, keep the hope in your hands like something carved.
Redeemer. In Hebrew, go'el: the family member who buys back what was lost and stands up for you when no one else will.
Your line: my redeemer lives. Job said it with no one left on his side. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Job 19:25 stands among the opening sentences of the Anglican burial service as a confession of hope in the resurrection, and it is sung as the soprano aria "I know that my Redeemer liveth" in Handel's Messiah.
